items.title: Will AI Coding Eat Video Game Engines?
items.summary: When Travis McGeathy’s studio, Seeker Entertainment, ran out of funding in September, its game KinForge went down with it. KinForge was an online game built in Unreal Engine 5.7 and designed to run on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). With no one left to pay the server bill, the game became unplayable even for those few developers, including studio co-founder McGeathy, who had the code. Then, on a whim, McGeathy pointed Anthropic’s Claude Code at the project and asked it to make KinForge playable without AWS. After four hours of mostly hands-off work he had a build that let players host their own games. Claude added support for peer-to-peer play over both the Internet and a local area network. To McGeathy’s surprise, it also added persistent save states, a feature that lets players resume a game if they’re disconnected. Although KinForge is still built in Unreal Engine, developments like this could give companies that create game engines cause for concern. The conversion was accomplished with an agentic AI workflow that partially bypasses the elaborate, user-friendly game engine UI that many companies, including Unreal Engine creator Epic Games, have spent decades perfecting. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2, released November 9, further upped the ante. The model is capable of generating a 3D game with a custom game engine in the style of the hit Call of Duty series. This raises a question: can game engines evolve quickly enough to keep pace with model improvements? “We’re definitely in a world where I can just dream up software really fast. So, if Unreal Engine was static, what’s the value at the end of next year? This is why we are pivoting hard towards velocity,” says Daniel Vogel , chief operating officer at Epic Games. “I think with any fixed set of features or functionality, it can eventually be replicated. If we’re doing our job right, we’re pushing the engine and pushing the envelope forward.” From Code to Nodes, and Back Again Major game engines often offer developers new visual tools and workflows that help them build games while interacting with less code. Unreal Engine’s Blueprints, a graphically based system introduced in Unreal Engine 4 that lets designers script gameplay simply by wiring boxes together, is an example. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , an award-winning game from French studio Sandfall Interactive, leaned heavily on Blueprints for scripting gameplay encounters . That should have been proof of the feature’s success. Instead, Epic will remove Blueprints in Unreal Engine 6 (UE6). Why? Blame LLMs. “AI doesn’t handle Blueprints very well,” says McGeathy. “It would much rather work with the code.” Currently, LLMs interact with Unreal Engine primarily through a Model Context Protocol server . MCP is an open-source standard created by Anthropic that lets AI send commands to software. “It’s not actually moving the mouse,” says Ryan Barker , a gameplay and systems engineer who has worked on projects for Amazon Games and Sony Online Entertainment. “It’s sending signals to the editor that the editor understands.” UE6 will lean into that reality by moving all code to Verse, a text-based programming language that will replace both Blueprints and Unreal Engine 5’s C++ gameplay framework. UE6 will also replace Unreal’s actor framework, which is based on object-oriented programming , with Scene Graph, which resembles an entity component system . “Typically, an ECS is a lot harder to code around,” says Barker, but ECS can provide superior game performance and result in less duplicate code . An LLM can help manage the complexity. Verse debuted in Unreal Editor for Fortnite in 2023, while Scene Graph arrived in 2024. Verse was designed to let millions of creators run code side by side in Fortnite, so it’s strict. The compiler catches mistakes before code runs and limits what each function can do. And because Scene Graph is built on Verse, an AI can work with a game world through code. That’s different from Blueprints, which are stored as binary files that LLMs can’t read directly. In addition to these changes, UE6 will make the engine more modular and expose its systems through an application programming interface “so that AI tooling can get at them without needing to fall back to slow computer use,” says Marcus Wassmer , the executive vice president of development at Epic Games. An internal effort that Epic calls “Python All The Things” aims to make everything in the editor scriptable. UE6 will also store more game assets as text so an LLM can edit them directly. For binary assets (non-text files) that remain, Epic is building a command-line tool that allows agents to interact with the files without loading the full UE6 interface. The traditional Unreal Engine editor isn’t going away, but Vogel expects it will change as LLM use becomes more common. “You’re not going to move stuff visually in the editor. Those times are gone,” he says. Instead, he expects game developers will more frequently use the Unreal Engine editor to visualize “the context needed to make decisions, or make the tweaks.” Unreal Engine 5.9 offers a glimpse at what that transition will mean in practice. Released as a developer preview on 9 November , it includes a new feature called Unreal Canvas . Vogel says it’s a collaboration feature that takes inspiration from visual workspace software like Miro . “It’s a way to make sense of the project,” says Vogel. Why Buy an Engine When You Can Build One? Epic Games’ goal is to keep Unreal Engine relevant in a world where AI coding tools are becoming ever-more capable. The company has the benefit of approaching the problem from a position of strength : Unreal Engine is the second most commonly used engine, after Unity Technologies’ Unity engine, and ranks first if measured by the number of games sold. Will that be enough? McGeathy says there can be benefits to creating an engine from scratch. “If you own the engine, you’re not reliant on a third party who could yank it out from underneath you.” However, he remains skeptical that many developers will go that route, even if AI makes it less painful. “Your goal as a game developer is to make a game. It’s not to make a game engine.” What LLMs do change, he says, is to lower the cost of switching between game engines. McGeathy, an Unreal veteran, used Claude to start building in Godot , an open-source engine he had never touched himself. “AI made transitioning from using Unreal into Godot trivial,” he says. Barker agrees. He used an LLM to build physics test scenes in both Unreal and Godot, which let him evaluate which engine was better suited to handle a game concept. Wassmer recognizes that AI makes it “easier [for developers using Unreal Engine] to pick up a new standard, or to convert stuff,” and says that Epic won’t attempt to block this shift. On the contrary, UE6 will remove barriers where possible. “Our explicit goal is to be able to interoperate with other ecosystems and other games,” he says. He feels confident that, even with the aid of LLMs, building an engine from scratch carries a heavy price that most developers won’t want to pay. “You still have to burn a lot of tokens to get something of scale that is optimized and that runs across all platforms,” Wassmer says. “Would you rather spend that time and energy building something from scratch? Or would you rather use something modular, like UE6, and trim out the bits you don’t need?”

items.title: Startup Makes Headway Towards Formalizing All of Math With AI
items.summary: As Axiom Math ’s AI swarm was putting the final touches on the automatic verification of 15,000-page proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG) , colloquially referred to as the ‘enormous theorem’, on Sunday 25 October, the company’s Founding Mathematician Ken Ono had nothing to do but watch and reflect on the achievement. As the son of a mathematician , he had grown up surrounded by some of the architects of the CFSG’s proof, widely considered to be the longest mathematical proof ever written by humans. Now, he was contributing to formally verifying what his father and peers had created. “My wife was with me as I watched the team countdown to completing the verification,” he recalls. “God, I cannot tell you how emotional I was.” University of St Andrews group theorist Colva Roney-Dougal (who was not involved in the work) says of formalizing CFSG: “I held it up as an example of something that was going to be incredibly hard to formalize because I had thought that the amount of computing it was going to require was just unattainable,” she says. “So when I heard the announcement, I was really, really surprised.” This result, along with the concurrent formal verification of the 7500-page Stacks project , represent a huge AI engineering achievement and lay some of the groundwork for digitizing all mathematics. Formally enormous Why the hoo-ha? The CFSG concerns finite simple groups. These are groups (sets of elements combined with an operation, like addition or multiplication, that follows specific rules) that are simple (in other words, cannot be reduced or simplified further) and finite (as opposed to groups containing an infinite number of elements). For example, all the permutations of a deck of cards form a simple finite group. Évariste Galois laid the foundations for group theory almost 200 years ago. Finite simple groups have since been classified by myriad mathematicians into 18 families (plus 26 sporadic simple groups that do not belong to any of these families). The CFSG’s proof confirms that this list is complete. But this simple task was only achieved by bringing together results and arguments that far exceed what any individual mathematician can fully absorb from more than 500 journal articles written by around 100 authors over a half-century period. Translating this interconnected web of knowledge into code and verifying its correctness therefore posed a number of significant engineering challenges, even beyond those overcome in earlier proof formalizations by Axiom Math this year . One of the hardest, according to Axiom Math’s Niels Voss , who led the CFSG formalization, was the sheer length of the proof. Over 15,000 pages of dense mathematics, the CFSG proof contains multiple theorems, lemmas, and definitions none of which can be checked until everything has been made machine-readable. To get around this required some ingenuity. “We processed all the literature from the CFSG, and traced the network structure of the informal proof before we were able to start working on it,” says Voss. “We then broke up the statement of the CFSG into about 100 milestones—landmark results along the way that can be independently verified—which we used to guide the formalization and stay on track.” Roney-Dougal says she is very impressed with the result, and particularly appreciates how the formal proof finds and clears up several mistakes in the original human proof. She thinks this result is critical to formalizing any modern research in group theory, such as her own work understanding how simple finite groups behave. But, Roney-Dougal says, because the verification was done automatically, there are few mathematicians capable of extracting information from the proof to share with the community, and that a new generation of mathematicians may have “missed a chance to gain knowledge from the doing of it”. Stacks of ingenuity required Just nine days after the CFSG formalization announcement, Axion Math revealed it had automatically formalized the Stacks project, too. Started in 2005 by Columbia University mathematician Aise Johan de Jong , Stacks is a massive, open-source collaborative mathematics textbook and reference work focused on highly abstract algebraic geometry and algebraic stacks (geometric spaces that are vital to modern string theory and number theory). Whereas CFSG is a single (huge) landmark theorem, the Stacks project is essentially a well-structured library of thousands of interlocking definitions, constructions, and lemmas bringing all of modern algebraic geometry together. The final Stacks formalization stands at a mere 16 million lines of code (compared to CFSG’s 43 million lines of code, roughly on a par with the Linux kernel), but it presented a different challenge to Axiom Math engineers: needing to achieve faithfulness and coherence across thousands of interlocking definitions and theorems, says Axiom Math’s Vasily Ilin , who led the project. This required the team to design a hierarchical system of AI agents with specialized responsibilities working in parallel, keeping every definition aligned across the library, while also checking faithfulness with multi-agent audits, cross-checks against sources, and hard tests. This ensured that every element and task aligned across the entire project. A highly efficient, general, reusable, and maintainable formal library of foundational concepts underpinning much of modern mathematics, the impact of the Stacks formalization could be profound. Now, anyone or any bot can access the formal Stacks library and build new formal mathematics upon it. And together, the CFSG and Stacks formalizations represent a significant step toward formalizing all of mathematics. “They show the two ways formalization has to scale: one very long proof, and one very wide body of connected theory,” says Ono. Ono and Voss see numerous advantages to a future in which formal mathematics becomes central: rubber stamping theorems and proofs, preserving knowledge as expertise dwindles over time, and building a shared library as a basis for creating new mathematics. They are also optimistic about humanity’s role when all of mathematics is formalized, viewing formalization as a launchpad for humans to use and understand mathematics in new and innovative ways. “Aren’t we excited to think more broadly about what the future of math can be?,” asks Ono. “I’m excited by that. I’m really excited.”
